doc.title: Jim Cullum interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Is traditional jazz alive and well?
summary: Cullum says traditional jazz still has opportunities, though its WWII-generation audience is dying off.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: I was fortunate enough to be able to hear your presentation this morning talking about traditional jazz, and they called it alive and well. Do you think it’s alive and well?

I think there are opportunities, just like there are in any area, to do things with it and present it and carry it forward. I don’t think it’s dead on the table like some people feel like it is. Because there are problems in presenting it that it’s not the game is over. I just don’t think that you have to accept it and we have to reinvent the whole business all the time.
Problems in presenting it would you say?

Well I mean it has been buoyed up for a long time by people that are of the World War II generation who are now dying off. And people that heard — this whole generation that heard jazz at Eddie Condon’s and Nick’s in the Village and were also fans of the big bands and that were devotees of Artie Shaw or the Bob Crosby band or whatever. Those people are now all in their eighties if they’re still around. And so there’s not much opportunity – the music can’t be carried forward very much further on the strength of those people’s good will and taste.
